newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia shocks market, cuts rates by 0.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: Australia shocks market, cuts rates by 0.5 pct.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) on Wednesday shocked financial markets with a cut in official interest rates of 0.5 percentage points to 6.0 percent.
Rates were last cut on November 6 when the official cash rate was brought down to 6.5 percent from 7.0 percent.
"This reduction essentially reflects a further improvement in the inflationary outlook," said RBA governor Ian MacFarlane.

MacFarlane said the bank now expected inflation to stay below 2.5 percent for the remainder of 1996/97, citing the strength in the Australian dollar and recent national accounts data which suggested actual inflation could fall further.

The Australian dollar fell sharply in hectic morning trade after the bank's surprise move. By 9.33 am (2233 GMT) the local dollar had tumbled to US$0.7958/68 from an early US$0.8015.20 and US$0.8020/25 late here on Tuesday.
On the crosses the currency crumbled to 90.01/11 yen from an early 90.90/00 and 91.09/19 late here Tuesday.
But MacFarlane warned that if wages were to rise appreciably, interest rates would also rise, referring back to the bank's 1994 decisions to hike rates three times to control inflation.
"Monetary policy would, in such circumstances, be set to preserve the favourable inflation outlook," MacFarlane said in a statement.
Stunned financial markets agreed with the bank's inflation outlook, but had expected it to keep monetary policy on hold until early 1997 when the next inflation data is released.

"A little surprised as to the timing," said Saul Eslake, chief economist with the ANZ Banking Group. "We had thought that if there were to be another rate cut it would have been in February rather than in December."
Chris Caton, chief economist at Bankers Trust Australia, welcomed the cut. "We were expecting this in early February after the next round of inflation data," Caton told Reuters.
"The growth outlook for the economy is quite weak and inflation news is good so this is the right decision, it's just a little earlier then we thought it was going to be," he said.

"This is possibily the last cut, we will get some pickup in growth over the course next year. Monetary policy history is littered with examples of one too many moves. This wasn't the one too many move, but the next one might be."
However, one economist suggested the bank may have acted prematurely. "There may be an element of panic in this cut," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist, with Macquarie Bank.

"It may have been more sensible to wait for the December quarter CPI (Consumer Price Index) data to confirm the low inflation outlook. They must be more concerned about the economy than we thought, and particularly employment."
Official data last week showed the Australian economy slowing to an annual growth of 3.8 percent from above five percent earlier in the year.
The government has been forecasting 2.0 percent employment growth and that by the end of the 1996/97 financial year (July/June) there would be a modest fall in unemployment.
